[[Image:DeWitt-Vilkovisky-Barvinsky-Quantum Gravity-V Moscow 1990.gif|thumb|right|Bryce S. DeWitt (center) with Grigori A. Vilkovisky (left) and Andrei O. Barvinsky (right) at the 5th Seminar on Quantum Gravity, Moscow, May 28 – June 1, 1990]]

'''Bryce Seligman DeWitt''' (born '''Carl Bryce Seligman'''; January 8, 1923 – September 23, 2004) was an American [[theoretical physicist]] noted for his work in [[gravitation]] and [[quantum field theory]].<ref name="weinberg">{{Cite web |last=Weinberg |first=Steven |date=2008 |title=Bryce Seligman DeWitt 1923-2004: Biographical Memoir |url= https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/dewitt-bryce.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2025| website=nasoline.org}}</ref>

==Personal life==
He was born Carl Bryce Seligman, but he and his three brothers, including noted ichthyologist [[Hugh Hamilton DeWitt]], added "DeWitt" from their mother's side of the family, at the urging of their father, in 1950. Several decades later, when [[Felix Bloch]] learned of this name change, he was so upset that he blocked DeWitt's appointment to [[Stanford University]]; consequently, DeWitt and his wife [[Cecile DeWitt-Morette]], a mathematical physicist, accepted faculty positions at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://web2.ph.utexas.edu/utphysicshistory/BryceSDeWitt.html |title = UTPhysicsHistorySite|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190620190641/https://web2.ph.utexas.edu/utphysicshistory/BryceSDeWitt.html|archive-date=June 20, 2019}}</ref> DeWitt trained in [[World War II]] as a naval aviator, but the war ended before he saw combat.  He died September 23, 2004, from [[pancreatic cancer]] at the age of 81. He is buried in [[France]], and was survived by his wife and four daughters.<ref>[https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/statesman/name/bryce-dewitt-obituary?id=27719201 Family Obituary]</ref><ref name="weinberg"/>

== Academic life ==
He received his bachelor's (''[[summa cum laude]]''), master's and doctoral degrees from [[Harvard University]]. His Ph.D. (1950) supervisor was [[Julian S. Schwinger]], a Nobel Prize-winning american theoretical physicist, best known for his work on [[quantum electrodynamics]] ([[Quantum electrodynamics|QED]]). Afterwards, DeWitt held a postdoctoral position at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton, New Jersey, and worked at the [[Lawrence Livermore Lab]] (1952–1955). Thereafter, he held faculty positions at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] (1956–1972) and, later, at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] (1973–2004).

In 1957 he and his wife organized the [[Chapel Hill Conference]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Halpern |first=Paul |date=2013 |title=The Role of the 1957 Chapel Hill Conference in the History of General Relativity |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013APS..APRT15006H/abstract |journal=APS April Meeting Abstracts |volume=2013 |pages=T15.006 |bibcode=2013APS..APRT15006H }}</ref>

=== Awards ===
In 1987 he was awarded the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Prize]],<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20080103113108/http://users.ictp.it/~sci_info/awards/Dirac/DiracMedallists/DiracMedal87.html Dirac Prize citation], [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]]</ref> the [[Pomeranchuk Prize]] in 2002, and, posthumously, the American Physical Society's [[Einstein Prize (APS)|Einstein Prize]]  in 2005.<ref>[http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?name=Bryce%20DeWitt&year=2005 Einstein Prize citation], [[American Physical Society]]</ref>  He also was a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=DeWitt, Bryce S. (Bryce Seligman), 1923-2004 |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11506026.html |access-date=October 7, 2023 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref>

=== Work ===
He pioneered work in the quantization of [[general relativity]] and, in particular, developed [[canonical quantum gravity]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=DeWitt |first=Bryce S. |date=1967 |title=Quantum Theory of Gravity. I. The Canonical Theory |url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.160.1113 |journal=Physical Review |volume=160 |issue=5 |pages=1113–1148 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.160.1113|bibcode=1967PhRv..160.1113D |url-access=subscription }}</ref> manifestly covariant methods, and heat kernel algorithms. DeWitt formulated the [[Wheeler–DeWitt equation]] for the [[wave function of the universe]] with [[John Archibald Wheeler]] and advanced the formulation of [[Hugh Everett]]'s [[many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics]].<ref name="weinberg"/> With his student [[Larry Smarr]], he originated the field of [[numerical relativity]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=DeWitt-Morette |first1=Cécile |title=The Pursuit of Quantum Gravity: Memoirs of Bryce DeWitt from 1946 to 2004 |date=2011 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-642-14270-3 |pages=51–117 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-14270-3_4 |language=en |chapter=Quantum Gravity |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-14270-3_4 }}</ref>{{rp|25–35,37}}

* Bryce DeWitt, [[R. Neill Graham]], eds., ''The Many-Worlds Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics'', Princeton Series in Physics, [[Princeton University Press]] (1973), {{ISBN|0-691-08131-X}}.
* S. M. Christensen, ed., ''Quantum theory of gravity. Essays in honor of the 60th birthday of Bryce S. DeWitt'', Adam Hilger, Bristol, 1984.
* Bryce DeWitt, ''Supermanifolds'', Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 1985.
* Bryce DeWitt, ''The Global Approach to Quantum Field Theory'', The International Series of Monographs on Physics, [[Oxford University Press]], 2003, {{ISBN|978-0-19-851093-2}}.
* Bryce DeWitt, ''Sopra un raggio di luce'', Di Renzo Editore, Roma, 2005.
* Bryce DeWitt, ''Bryce DeWitt's Lectures on Gravitation'', Steven M. Christensen, ed., Springer, 2011.
